findings.title: Salesforce refresh path references an undeclared Prisma client
findings.body: The new refresh path calls `prisma.credential.update`, but this file does not import `prisma`. TypeScript will fail with `Cannot find name 'prisma'`, blocking the app-store type check/build before this feature can be deployed.

findings.title: Sync mode returns an unparsed Fetch Response to handlers expecting provider data
findings.body: When credential syncing is enabled, this function returns the native `fetch` Response directly instead of the type returned by each provider's `refreshFunction`. Google reads `res.data`, HubSpot treats the result as a `HubspotToken`, and Zoho/Bigin read Axios-style `tokenInfo.data`; a standard Response has none of those properties and its JSON body is never read. Enabling the sync endpoint therefore causes undefined-token failures or TypeErrors for those integrations.

findings.title: The minimal sync-response schema discards expiry fields and overwrites refresh tokens
findings.body: `z.string().toString()` is not a wildcard object key: both computed keys evaluate to `"[object Object]"`. Consequently this Zod object strips normal unknown fields such as `expiry_date`/`expires_in`, so a sync response containing the documented access token and expiry retains only `access_token`; line 26 then inserts the literal `"refresh_token"`. Consumers persist that placeholder (for example Office and Zoom), corrupting the real refresh token and losing the new expiry, so later refreshes—especially after sync is disabled—cannot authenticate correctly.

findings.title: Google refresh stores the SafeParse wrapper instead of credential keys
findings.body: `parseRefreshTokenResponse` returns Zod's `SafeParseReturnType` (`{ success, data }`), but this value is written directly as `Credential.key`. The next GoogleCalendarService construction parses `credential.key` as a Google credential object and instead receives the wrapper, so any Google credential refreshed through this path becomes unusable. This occurs even when credential syncing is disabled because this helper is now always used.

findings.title: Zoho Bigin sends the credential record ID as the Cal.com user ID
findings.body: `refreshOAuthTokens` serializes its third argument as `calcomUserId`, but this call passes `credentialId`, which is the Credential table primary key rather than `credential.userId`. The external credential source will look up the wrong user; it may return no token or, if that numeric ID belongs to another user, a token that is then saved onto the current user's credential.

findings.title: Salesforce ignores the configured credential-sync endpoint
findings.body: Unlike the other modified integrations, the Salesforce refresh path always calls Salesforce directly and never calls `refreshOAuthTokens` or checks `CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT`. Thus, even with credential syncing enabled, Salesforce continues using the locally stored refresh token rather than the self-hoster's source of truth, leaving this integration unsupported by the advertised feature.

findings.title: Concurrent credential webhooks can create duplicate credentials
findings.body: The handler performs `findFirst` followed by a separate `create` when no credential is found. Two simultaneous deliveries for the same user and app can both observe no row and both create one; the comment confirms there is no usable unique key for an upsert. Future syncs then update an arbitrary `findFirst` result, while duplicate credentials can lead to ambiguous or duplicate integration behavior.

findings.title: The new credential-sync security and refresh flows have no automated coverage
findings.body: No tests were added for this new authenticated, encrypted webhook or for the enabled/disabled refresh branches. Tests should at least cover rejecting invalid secrets, decrypting and idempotently creating/updating credentials, and consuming the sync endpoint's normal JSON response; the current unparsed-response and token-corruption regressions would have been caught by such coverage.
